opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the practical challenges split into a few buckets, and latency is probably the most immediate one. These models are big, and a robot moving through a warehouse with people and forklifts around can't wait a second or two for the model to figure out what it's looking at. So you end up with a layered setup: the vision-language model handles the higher-level reasoning, like "which bin is this, what's the task, is something unusual here," and a much faster, smaller policy runs the actual motion and balance at high frequency. Getting those two layers to talk to each other cleanly is a real engineering problem.

Compute and power on the robot are the second issue. You'd love to run everything onboard so you're not depending on warehouse Wi-Fi, which is often worse than people expect with all those metal racks. But onboard compute costs battery and adds heat, so there's constant tension between running locally, offloading to the cloud, or distilling the model into something smaller.

The third is reliability. A VLM demo can look impressive when it's right ninety-five percent of the time. In a warehouse running three shifts, that remaining five percent means a lot of failures every day. So a lot of the work goes into knowing when the model is uncertain, falling back to safe behavior, and making sure a confused language model can never override the low-level safety layer. Lighting changes, reflective shrink-wrap, damaged boxes, and labels in odd places all show up constantly in real facilities and much less in training data.

Then there's the data question. Internet-scale pretraining gives these models general knowledge, but it doesn't know your customer's specific layout or SKUs. You need a good pipeline for collecting data from deployed robots, finding the failure cases, and feeding them back in without breaking what already works.

So I'm optimistic. The semantic understanding these models bring is a big step up from hand-engineered perception. But the gap between a working demo and a system you can deploy is mostly about latency, robustness, and safety architecture, and less about the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response notes that cloud offloading depends on warehouse Wi‑Fi and contrasts it with onboard inference, but it does not identify the alternative of installing servers in the warehouse.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that my background is really on the locomotion and control side, so I come at this from the perspective of someone who has spent a lot of time getting policies to run reliably on actual hardware, and that colors how I think about it.

The first practical issue is just latency and compute. A vision-language model, even a small one, is running at maybe a few hertz, and often that's on a GPU that isn't on the robot at all. Meanwhile the low-level controller on a legged or wheeled platform needs to run at hundreds of hertz and it cannot wait. So you end up with this hierarchy almost by necessity: the VLM does slow, high-level reasoning, and something much faster and much dumber handles the actual motion. The interesting engineering is in the interface between those two layers. What does the VLM output? A waypoint, a skill selection, a language instruction to a lower-level policy? Each of those choices has very different failure modes.

The second issue is reliability in the boring sense. In a warehouse you're doing the same kinds of tasks thousands of times a day, and the economics only work if the failure rate is extremely low. VLMs are impressive on the long tail, they can handle a weird object or an unusual instruction, but they are not yet consistent on the ninety-nine percent case. They'll hallucinate an object that isn't there, or confidently misjudge a distance. And when a model is wrong in a way that's hard to predict, it's hard to build a safety layer around it. With a classical pipeline, at least you know roughly where it breaks.

Third, there's the distribution shift problem, which is familiar from sim-to-real work. These models are trained largely on internet images, and a warehouse is a very particular visual world: repetitive shelving, bad lighting, lots of occlusion, barcodes and labels that matter a lot but are tiny in the frame. Fine-tuning helps, but collecting the data on a deployed fleet, labeling it, and then validating that the new model hasn't regressed somewhere else is a real operational burden that people underestimate.

And then the last thing I'd flag is connectivity and the question of where the model lives. If you put it in the cloud, you've got network dropouts and the robot has to degrade gracefully. If you put it on the robot, you're fighting power and thermal budgets, and on a mobile platform every watt you give to inference is a watt you're not giving to the actuators.

So my honest view is that VLMs are very useful today for the parts of the problem that are genuinely open-ended: understanding an instruction from a human, dealing with an unexpected situation, maybe planning at the task level. But the bulk of what makes a warehouse robot work is still fast, well-tuned, fairly conventional control and perception, and I think the near-term wins come from combining those carefully rather than trying to replace them.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cloud inference network dropouts and on-robot power and thermal costs, but does not identify the fleet-level tradeoff of needing strong internet connectivity or installing servers in the warehouse.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is closing the gap between understanding a scene and reliably acting in it. A vision-language model might recognize a box or interpret an instruction, but the robot still needs to know where to grasp, whether it can reach safely, and what to do if the box moves or the grasp fails.

In a warehouse, you also have latency and compute constraints. If you send images to a remote model, you introduce a dependency on the network. If you run everything onboard, you have to fit within the robot’s compute and power budget. So I’d separate the higher-level reasoning from the fast control loop. The vision-language model can help decide what to do, while a dedicated controller handles the motion.

And then there’s reliability. You have changing lighting, occlusions, damaged packaging, people moving around. The question isn’t just whether the model succeeds on a demonstration. It’s whether the system can recognize when it doesn’t have enough information, stop safely, and recover. That’s where a lot of the practical engineering comes in.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key challenge is closing the gap between understanding a scene and acting reliably in it. A vision-language model might recognize a box or understand an instruction, but the robot still needs to know where it can move, whether it can grasp that box, and what to do if something changes.

In a warehouse, you also have practical constraints: compute, latency, changing lighting, occlusions, and people moving around. You can’t have the robot waiting unpredictably for a model response while it’s executing a motion. So I would separate the higher-level reasoning from the fast control loop. The model can help interpret a task or choose the next action, while a more constrained controller handles execution.

And then there’s recovery. When the model is uncertain or the grasp fails, can the robot recognize that, get another observation, and try again safely? That’s a big part of making these systems useful outside a demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response mentions compute and latency constraints but does not identify the offboard-inference tradeoff of requiring strong internet connectivity or installing warehouse servers.
